w7.title: Reliability in the Cloud Era
w7.subtitle: Static stability, cells, %1%, %2% and multi-region survival.
w7.intro:
The %1% book was written from inside %2%'s own infrastructure. This world covers the practices that the industry (and %3% in particular) developed for the same problems on rented infrastructure: %4% and the control-plane/data-plane split, %5% and %6% for blast-radius reduction, %7% as a discipline, multi-region disaster recovery with honest recovery objectives, and the measurement practices that connect reliability to delivery performance.

Sources here are the %8% %9% reliability pillar, the %10% Builders' Library, the %11% research programme, and the workbook's cloud chapters, alongside the book's own material.

The final boss is a region impairment: everything from all seven worlds, at once.
w7.l1.title: Static stability and the %1%
w7.l1.summary: Why systems should keep working without making new decisions, and what that costs.
w7.l1.body:
## The split

Every cloud system has two planes:

- The **%2%** creates and changes things: launching instances, changing a load balancer's targets, updating %3% records, modifying %4%. It is low-volume, complex, and correspondingly more likely to be impaired.
- The **%5%** does the recurring work: routing packets, serving requests from running instances, resolving already-published %6% answers, reading objects.

Data planes are generally far more reliable than control planes, because they are simpler and because they are designed to keep doing what they were last told. %7% designs services this way deliberately, and publishes the distinction so that customers can build on it.

%1%

## The principle

**Static stability** means a system continues to operate correctly during a failure without needing to make changes, and therefore without needing the %8%. The classic formulation: the system keeps working with the resources it already has, even if it cannot provision, modify or discover anything new.

The consequences are concrete and often uncomfortable:

- **Pre-provision for failure.** If you run three %9% and must survive losing one, run enough capacity in all three that the remaining two can serve 100% of traffic *right now*, without waiting for %10%. That means running at roughly 50 to 66% utilisation in normal operation and paying for it.
- **Do not depend on scaling as a disaster response.** Scaling up during an %11% event requires the %12% %13% at exactly the moment it is busiest, and takes minutes you do not have.
- **Cache what you must look up.** A request path that calls a discovery service, a configuration API or an %14% endpoint on every request inherits that dependency's availability. Cache with a long enough %15% that the dependency can be down for a while without user impact, and fail open to the last known value.
- **Prefer pre-created resources.** Pre-warmed connection pools, pre-created queues, pre-published %16% records with health-check-based failover rather than records created during the event.

## The bimodal-behaviour warning

The Builders' Library makes a related point: systems that behave one way normally and a different way during failure are dangerous, because the failure mode is rarely exercised. A failover path that only runs during a disaster is a path you have never tested at load. Static stability reduces the number of modes: ideally the system does the same thing during an %17% failure as it does on a Tuesday, just with fewer machines.

## Where it conflicts with cost

The honest trade-off: %18% costs idle capacity. The counter-argument is the %19%. If surviving an %20% loss is worth more than the idle capacity costs, pre-provision; if not, accept the exposure explicitly and write it down. What is not acceptable is assuming %21% will save you and never testing it.

> [aws]**On %22%.** Practical rules: set %23% group minimum capacity so that the surviving %24% can carry full load, not just the desired capacity you would need on a normal day. Use %25% with cross-zone load balancing so an %26%'s loss redistributes automatically. Prefer %27% health checks with pre-created failover records over %28% changes made during an incident. For %29%, understand that a failover is a control-plane action with a real duration; for %30% global tables, writes continue in the surviving region without a promotion step. Cache %31% and configuration lookups. Use %32% warm pools if launch time matters. And check the dependency you forgot: if your instances fetch a configuration file from %33% at boot, a boot during an %34% event is a boot that fails.
w7.l1.q0.q: What does "%1%" mean for a system running across three %2%?
w7.l1.q0.explain: Static stability is the ability to keep operating correctly without making new decisions or new resources during the failure.
w7.l1.q0.c0: The system never changes its configuration
w7.l1.q0.c1: The system survives the loss of one %1% using capacity it is already running, without needing the %2% to provision anything
w7.l1.q0.c2: The system uses static IP addresses
w7.l1.q0.c3: The system scales automatically when an %1% fails
w7.l1.q1.q: A service runs across 3 %1% and must serve 100% of traffic after losing any one %2%, using only already-running capacity. What is the maximum average utilisation per %3% in normal operation, as a percentage? (Whole number.)
w7.l1.q1.explain: Two %1% must carry 100%, so each %2% runs at most 50% of total load, meaning the fleet as a whole runs at about 2/3 (67%) of its capacity.
w7.l1.q1.hint: Two of three %1% must carry all the load.
w7.l1.q2.q: Why is relying on %1% as the primary response to an %2% failure risky?
w7.l1.q2.explain: Scaling is a control-plane action with latency. Pre-provisioned capacity is the statically stable answer; scaling handles growth, not disasters.
w7.l1.q2.c1: It depends on the %1% %2% at the moment it is most stressed, and takes minutes during which the surviving %3% are overloaded
w7.l1.q3.q: Which design detail would violate %1% for a request path?
w7.l1.q3.explain: A per-request control-plane call inherits that plane's availability. Cache it, with a %1% long enough to ride out an impairment.
w7.l1.q3.c0: Reading a cached configuration value from memory
w7.l1.q3.c1: Calling a service-discovery API on every incoming request
w7.l1.q4.q: True or false: a failover path that only executes during a disaster is safer than one exercised in normal operation, because it is simpler.
w7.l1.q4.explain: False. Bimodal behaviour means the disaster path is the least-tested code in the system. Prefer designs where failure changes the scale of operation, not its mode.
w7.l2.title: Blast radius: cells and %1%
w7.l2.summary: Partitioning a service so that a failure affects a fraction of customers rather than all of them.
w7.l2.body:
## The problem with one big fleet

A single fleet serving all customers has a single %2%: any poison input, memory leak, bad deploy or noisy neighbour affects everyone. Redundancy within the fleet does not help, because every replica runs the same code against the same workload.

## Cell-based architecture

A **cell** is a complete, independent instance of the service stack: its own compute, its own data store, its own capacity. Customers (or partitions of the workload) are assigned to a cell. A thin routing layer maps a request to its cell.

Properties this buys:

- **Bounded %3%.** A failure inside a cell affects that cell's customers only. With 10 cells, the default impact of a cell-level failure is 10% of customers instead of 100%.
- **Bounded scale.** Each cell is a known size, tested at that size. You scale by adding cells, so you never discover a new scaling limit in production.
- **Safer deployments.** Deploy cell by cell, which is a %4% with a naturally bounded population and a natural rollback unit.
- **Testable capacity.** You can load-test one cell to destruction and know what the whole system does.

The costs: the routing layer becomes critical (keep it thin, simple and statically stable), per-cell overhead multiplies fixed costs, and cross-cell operations (a customer moving, or a query spanning cells) need explicit design. Cells work best when the workload partitions naturally by tenant.

## Shuffle sharding

Shuffle sharding refines the assignment. Instead of giving each customer one cell, give each customer a random *combination* of nodes or cells.

%1%

With 8 nodes and a shard size of 2, there are 28 possible pairs. A customer sending poison traffic degrades only its own two nodes. Every other customer shares at most one node with them, so with a retry to the healthy node, most customers see no failure at all. The chance that another customer has exactly the same pair is 1 in 28.

The arithmetic generalises: with *n* nodes and shard size *k*, there are "n choose k" shards. Eight nodes and shard size 2 gives 28; 100 nodes with shard size 5 gives over 75 million. The fraction of customers sharing a complete shard with a victim becomes vanishingly small, while each customer still only uses *k* nodes' worth of resources.

Requirements for it to work: the client must retry across the nodes in its shard, the workload must be partitionable per customer, and the shard assignment must be stable (usually a hash of the customer ID).

## Choosing a partition key

Cells and shards are only as good as the key. Common choices: customer or tenant ID, account ID, or a geographic region. Bad choices create hot cells (a key where one value dominates) or make routing stateful. Plan for rebalancing, and for the one customer who outgrows a cell.

> [aws]**On %5%.** Cell routing can be as simple as %6% records per cell plus a lookup service, or an %7% with host-based routing. %8%'s own services use both patterns extensively: %9%'s infrastructure uses %10% across its name servers, and many %11% services are internally cell-based per %12% or per region partition. For your own workloads, the natural cell boundary is often an %13% account plus a %14% per cell, which gives you quota isolation and %15% isolation for free. Keep the routing layer's %16% statically stable: a cached mapping that survives the lookup service being down.

## When not to cellularise

If the workload does not partition (a global leaderboard, a single shared graph), cells add complexity without bounding the %17%. If you have ten customers, the arithmetic does not help. Start with AZ-level and region-level isolation, and reach for cells when tenant count and the cost of a full outage both justify it.
w7.l2.q0.q: What is the defining property of a cell in %1%?
w7.l2.q0.explain: Independence is the point: its own compute and data, so a failure inside it cannot reach other cells.
w7.l2.q0.c0: A cell is a single server
w7.l2.q0.c1: A cell is a complete, independent instance of the service stack serving an assigned subset of customers
w7.l2.q0.c2: A cell is a database shard shared by all application servers
w7.l2.q0.c3: A cell is an availability zone
w7.l2.q1.q: With 9 nodes and a shuffle-shard size of 2, how many distinct shards (node pairs) are possible?
w7.l2.q1.hint: n choose k = n(n−1)/2 for k = 2
w7.l2.q2.q: A customer sends poison traffic that crashes both nodes in their shuffle shard. Why do most other customers see little or no impact?
w7.l2.q2.explain: Overlap is partial for almost everyone, and client retry across the shard converts partial overlap into no user-visible failure.
w7.l2.q2.c1: Each other customer shares at most one of those two nodes, so a retry reaches their healthy node; only a customer with the identical pair is fully affected
w7.l2.q2.c2: Other customers are on different regions
w7.l2.q2.c3: The load balancer detects poison traffic
w7.l2.q3.q: Which are genuine costs or requirements of %1%? Select all that apply.
w7.l2.q3.explain: Cells make deployment safer but do not remove the need for staged rollout; they give it a natural unit.
w7.l2.q3.c0: A routing layer that must be kept thin and highly available
w7.l2.q3.c2: Explicit design for cross-cell operations and customer migration
w7.l2.q3.c3: It removes the need for %1% deployments
w7.l2.q3.c4: A workload that partitions naturally by tenant
w7.l2.q4.q: Which workload is the poorest fit for cell-based partitioning?
w7.l2.q4.explain: A globally shared mutable structure does not partition, so cells add complexity without bounding the %1%.
w7.l2.q4.c0: A multi-tenant SaaS API with 50,000 customers
w7.l2.q4.c2: A single global leaderboard that every user reads and writes
w7.l3.title: Chaos engineering and %1%
w7.l3.summary: Running experiments on production systems to find the failures before they find you.
w7.l3.body:
## The discipline

Chaos engineering is the practice of running deliberate experiments on a system to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions. It is not "randomly break things"; it is a scientific method with a safety envelope.

The canonical loop:

1. **Define steady state** as a measurable output that indicates normal behaviour. Use the %1%: success rate, latency percentile, order-completion rate. "The service is up" is not a steady-state definition.
2. **Hypothesise** that steady state will continue during the injected condition. State it explicitly: "when one %2%'s instances are terminated, success rate stays above 99.9% and %3% stays below 400 ms".
3. **Inject a realistic fault**: instance termination, %4% impairment, dependency latency, API throttling, disk pressure, certificate expiry, clock skew.
4. **Try to disprove the hypothesis** by measuring the steady-state metrics during the experiment.
5. **Stop** automatically if the %5% exceeds the agreed limit.

## The rules that keep it safe

- **Minimise %6%.** Start in a test environment, then a single cell or a small percentage of production traffic. Expand only after the small experiment passes.
- **Define stop conditions before starting**, wired to automation, not to a human watching a dashboard. An experiment that cannot abort itself is an outage waiting for permission.
- **Run during business hours** with the owning team present. Chaos at 3 a.m. teaches you about your pager, not your system.
- **Announce it.** An unannounced experiment that causes a real incident burns the trust the practice needs.
- **Prefer production**, carefully. Staging does not have production's traffic, data volume or dependency graph, which is where the interesting failures live. Reaching production is the goal, not the starting point.

## Game days

A %7% is the human-scale version: a scheduled exercise where a team responds to an injected or simulated failure, practising the incident process from World 4 as well as the technical response. The value is in the second-order findings: the %8% that was out of date, the dashboard nobody could find, the escalation path that pointed at someone who left.

The **wheel of misfortune** variant is a tabletop exercise: a facilitator narrates a past incident, and the %9% engineer talks through what they would check and do. It costs an hour and no production risk, and is the cheapest way to fix operational underload.

## What to test first

Order the candidates by "how confident are we, and how bad would it be": loss of one %10%, a dependency returning errors, a dependency becoming slow (far more dangerous than down), a cache failing empty, a database failover, a certificate expiring, a quota being reached, the deployment pipeline being unavailable during an incident, and the restore path for your most important data.

Slow dependencies deserve special attention: World 5's cascade lesson is mostly about them, and a dependency that returns errors quickly is usually survivable while one that hangs is not.

> [aws]**On %11%.** %12% %13% runs experiments as code: stop or terminate instances, inject %14% or memory pressure, add latency or packet loss, throttle API calls to a service, fail over an %15% or %16% cluster, interrupt %17% instances, and (with the %18% availability-power-interruption action) simulate an %19% impairment. Every experiment template carries **stop conditions** bound to %20% alarms, which is the mechanism that makes production experiments defensible. Combine with %21% to define resilience policies with %22%/%23% targets and assess whether an architecture meets them. Keep experiment templates in version control next to the service they test, and run them on a schedule so resilience does not decay silently.
w7.l3.source: Principles of Chaos Engineering; %1% book ch.17; %2% FIS
w7.l3.q0.q: Put the %1% experiment loop in order.
w7.l3.q0.explain: Steady state, hypothesis, injection, measurement, with automated stop conditions throughout. Without a defined steady state there is nothing to disprove.
w7.l3.q0.i0: Define steady state as a measurable output (the %1%)
w7.l3.q0.i1: Hypothesise that steady state continues during the injected condition
w7.l3.q0.i2: Inject a realistic fault with a bounded %1%
w7.l3.q0.i3: Measure whether the hypothesis is disproved
w7.l3.q0.i4: Stop automatically if the %1% exceeds the limit, then act on findings
w7.l3.q1.q: Why does the lesson call a slow dependency more dangerous than one that is down?
w7.l3.q1.explain: This is the bimodal latency problem from World 5. Tight deadlines and fail-fast behaviour convert a dangerous failure mode into a survivable one.
w7.l3.q1.c0: Slow dependencies are harder to monitor
w7.l3.q1.c1: A fast failure frees the caller's resources; a hanging call ties up threads and connections until the caller collapses
w7.l3.q2.q: What makes a production chaos experiment defensible rather than reckless?
w7.l3.q2.explain: The safety envelope is what separates the discipline from an outage. Unannounced experiments destroy the trust the practice depends on.
w7.l3.q2.c0: Running it at night when traffic is low
w7.l3.q2.c1: A bounded %1%, automated stop conditions wired to alarms, the owning team present, and prior announcement
w7.l3.q2.c3: Running it without telling anyone so the response is realistic
w7.l3.q3.q: What is the main value of a "wheel of misfortune" tabletop exercise?
w7.l3.q3.explain: It is the cheapest remedy for operational underload, and the second-order findings (stale docs, wrong contacts) are usually the valuable part.
w7.l3.q3.c1: It gives %1% engineers realistic practice and exposes stale %2% and broken escalation paths at almost no risk
w7.l3.q4.q: Which %1% %2% feature most directly enforces the blast-radius rule?
w7.l3.q4.explain: Automated abort on an alarm is what lets an experiment run against production traffic without betting the %1% on a human watching a graph.
w7.l3.q4.c1: Stop conditions bound to %1% alarms that abort the experiment automatically
w7.l4.title: Multi-region strategy, %1% and %2%
w7.l4.summary: Four DR strategies, what they actually cost, and the dependencies people forget.
w7.l4.body:
## Two numbers first

- **%1% (Recovery Time Objective):** how long the service may be unavailable before the impact is unacceptable.
- **%2% (Recovery Point Objective):** how much recent data you may lose, expressed as time.

Both are business decisions with costs attached, exactly like an %3%. Stating them honestly is more than half the work: "%4% zero, %5% zero" is not a requirement, it is a refusal to choose.

## The four strategies

| Strategy | Typical %6% | Typical %7% | What runs in the second region |
|---|---|---|---|
| %8% and restore | Hours to a day | Hours | Nothing; backups are copied |
| Pilot light | Tens of minutes to hours | Minutes | Data replicated, core services off or minimal |
| Warm standby | Minutes | Seconds to minutes | A scaled-down but working copy serving nothing (or a trickle) |
| Multi-site active/active | Near zero | Near zero to seconds | Full capacity serving live traffic |

Cost rises with each row, and so does operational complexity. The key insight from the failure-mode literature: **the only failover you can trust is one you use routinely.** Active/active is expensive but continuously exercised; %9% is cheaper but its promotion path is bimodal (see lesson 7.1) unless you fail over on a schedule.

## Data is the hard part

Compute is easy to duplicate; state is not.

- **Asynchronous replication** gives a non-zero %10% by definition. Know the replication lag and monitor it as an %11%, because %12% is only as good as the lag at the moment of failure.
- **Synchronous replication** across regions costs write latency on every request, all the time, to protect against a rare event. Usually the wrong trade for cross-region; often the right one within a region.
- **Multi-writer designs** (%13% global tables) trade conflict resolution for availability: last-writer-wins is fine for some data and silently wrong for other data (counters, balances, inventory).
- **Failback** is the step people forget: after the primary region returns, how does data written in the secondary get reconciled? Design and test this, not just the failover.

## The dependencies people forget

- **%14% %15%** that are too long to fail over quickly, and resolvers that ignore them anyway.
- **Certificates, secrets and %16% keys** that exist only in the primary region. A %17% key is regional; data encrypted with it cannot be read elsewhere without a multi-region key or a re-encrypt step.
- **The deployment pipeline** living in the failed region, so you cannot ship the fix.
- **Identity**: if your IdP, or the %18% path your automation depends on, is impaired.
- **Third parties** that are themselves single-region.
- **Quotas in the standby region** that were never raised because nothing ever ran there at full scale.
- **Observability**: dashboards and alarms scoped to the primary region, leaving you blind exactly when you need to see.

## Deciding

Work backwards from the %19% and the business impact, not from the architecture diagram. A service with a 99.9% %20% has 43 minutes of budget a month; a four-hour %21% means a single regional event consumes six months of budget. That arithmetic, not an opinion about resilience, is the argument for spending on %22%.

> [aws]**On %23%.** %24% health checks with failover records, or %25% for faster, DNS-independent failover. %26% Global Database gives cross-region replication with typical lag under a second and a managed promotion (%27% seconds, %28% minutes); %29% global tables give active/active with last-writer-wins. %30% Cross-Region Replication with replication time control provides a measurable %31% for objects. %32% %33% copies vaults across regions and accounts. Use multi-region %34% keys for anything you must decrypt elsewhere. %35% %36% evaluates an architecture against stated %37%/%38% targets and flags the gaps. And practise: a scheduled regional failover exercise is the only evidence that the numbers in the table are real.
w7.l4.q0.explain: %1% is time to recover; %2% is the acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. Asynchronous replication makes %3% equal to the replication lag at the moment of failure.
w7.l4.q0.c1: How much recent data may be lost, expressed as a time window
w7.l4.q0.c3: The probability of a regional failure
w7.l4.q1.q: Which DR strategy keeps a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the workload running in the second region?
w7.l4.q1.explain: Pilot light keeps data replicated with services off or minimal; %1% runs a working, scaled-down copy that can be scaled up and cut over in minutes.
w7.l4.q2.q: A service has a 99.9% availability %1% over a 30-day window. A regional event causes a full outage lasting the full 4-hour %2%. How many months of %3% does that single event consume? (Round to a whole number.)
w7.l4.q2.explain: 240 minutes ÷ 43.2 minutes ≈ 5.6, so about 6 months of budget in one event. That arithmetic is the business case for a shorter %1%.
w7.l4.q3.q: Which of these are commonly forgotten cross-region dependencies? Select all that apply.
w7.l4.q3.explain: Keys, pipelines, quotas and observability are the classic gaps found during a real failover. %1% count is a design input, not a forgotten dependency.
w7.l4.q3.c0: %1% keys that exist only in the primary region
w7.l4.q3.c1: The deployment pipeline running in the failed region
w7.l4.q3.c2: Service quotas never raised in the standby region
w7.l4.q3.c3: Dashboards and alarms scoped only to the primary region
w7.l4.q3.c4: The number of %1% in the standby region
w7.l4.q4.q: Why does the lesson argue that a %1%'s failover path is riskier than active/active, beyond capacity?
w7.l4.q4.explain: Static stability's bimodal warning applies to DR directly. Either run active/active, or fail over on a schedule so the path is routine.
w7.l4.q4.c1: The promotion path is bimodal: it only runs during disasters, so it is the least-exercised code in the system
w7.l5.title: Measuring the practice: %1%, %2% and reliability economics
w7.l5.summary: Connecting reliability to delivery performance, and arguing for reliability work in the language of the business.
w7.l5.body:
## Two families of metric

%1% supplies **reliability outcomes**: %2% attainment, %3% consumption, pages per shift, time to detect, time to restore, %4% action-item closure. The %5% research programme supplies **delivery performance**:

- **Deployment frequency** — how often you ship to production.
- **Lead time for changes** — commit to running in production.
- **Change failure rate** — the fraction of deployments causing degraded service requiring remediation.
- **Failed deployment recovery time** — how long to restore service after a failed change.

The important finding, repeated across years of the research, is that these are **not in tension**. Teams that deploy more frequently, in smaller batches, with automated testing and progressive delivery, also have lower change failure rates and recover faster. Speed and stability rise together, and the practices that produce both are the ones in Worlds 3 and 4: small changes, staged rollout, fast rollback, good telemetry.

This is the empirical backing for the %6% argument. Slowing down is not the reliable choice; shipping small, reversible changes with good signals is.

## Using the numbers together

A useful quarterly picture per service:

| Question | Metric |
|---|---|
| Are users getting what we promised? | %7% attainment vs %8%, budget remaining |
| Are we spending the budget deliberately? | Budget consumed by incidents vs by launches |
| Is %9% sustainable? | Pages per shift, actionable ratio, incidents per shift |
| Are we learning? | Action-item closure rate, repeat-cause incidents |
| Can we change the system safely? | Deployment frequency, change failure rate, recovery time |

Report trends, not absolutes, and never rank teams against each other with them: a team with a hard problem will look worse than a team with an easy one, and the metrics will start being managed rather than measured.

## The economics argument

Reliability work competes with features for the same engineers. The argument that wins is arithmetic, not principle:

- Cost of the incident class: minutes of outage × revenue or cost per minute, plus the %10% consumed, plus the engineering hours spent responding.
- Cost of the fix: engineering time, plus any permanent infrastructure cost (the idle capacity of %11%, the second region).
- Probability and frequency, taken from your own incident history rather than from intuition.

Presented this way, "add a second region" and "fix the %12%" can be compared honestly, and the cheap fixes usually win by a wide margin. Most of the highest-value reliability work in this track (%13%, %14%, deadlines, %15% gates, tested restores) costs engineering time and almost no recurring infrastructure.

## What good looks like after all seven worlds

A service with: an %16% derived from user need, alerting derived from the %17%, a signed %18% policy, a paved-road deployment with %19% and one-click rollback, %20% and retry discipline, a bounded %21%, tested restores, a rehearsed incident process, blameless %22% with closed action items, and a rotation that fires about twice a shift and leaves time to fix things.

None of that is exotic. It is the accumulation of the decisions in this track, each one cheap on its own.

> [aws]**On %23%.** The measurement stack: %24% %25% for %26% attainment and %27%; %28% for anomaly surfacing; deployment metrics from %29% and %30% (or your CI) for %31%'s four; %32% or your ticketing system for incident counts and time to restore; %33% for the infrastructure side of the trade-off. %34% Tool reviews on a schedule turn the reliability pillar into tracked findings with owners, which is the same shape as %35% action items.
w7.l5.q0.q: Which are the four %1% delivery performance metrics? Select all that apply.
w7.l5.q0.explain: Error budget is an %1% reliability metric rather than a %2% delivery metric, though the two families are designed to be read together.
w7.l5.q1.q: What does the %1% research find about the relationship between delivery speed and stability?
w7.l5.q1.explain: This is the empirical basis for the %1% argument: the answer to instability is smaller, safer, more frequent changes, not fewer of them.
w7.l5.q1.c0: They trade off: faster delivery necessarily means lower stability
w7.l5.q1.c1: They rise together: teams shipping small changes frequently with automation also have lower change failure rates and recover faster
w7.l5.q1.c3: Stability improves only when deployment frequency falls
w7.l5.q2.q: Why does the lesson warn against ranking teams against each other using these metrics?
w7.l5.q2.explain: Comparative ranking creates an incentive to game the numbers, which destroys the signal. Report trends per service instead.
w7.l5.q2.c1: A team with a harder problem will look worse, and ranked metrics get managed rather than measured
w7.l5.q3.q: Which framing is most likely to win engineering time for reliability work?
w7.l5.q3.explain: Arithmetic using the organisation's own numbers is the argument that survives a prioritisation meeting. It also correctly ranks the cheap fixes first.
w7.l5.q3.c1: Cost of the incident class (outage minutes × cost per minute, budget consumed, response hours) compared against the cost of the fix, using your own incident history for frequency
w7.boss.title: Region Down
w7.boss.tagline: Everything you learned, on the worst day of the year, with the clock running.
w7.boss.intro:
You are the %1% for **Ledger**, a payments platform. Architecture: active in eu-west-1, %2% in eu-central-1. %3% Global Database (replication lag normally under 1 s), %4% global tables for session state, %5% with cross-region replication, %6% failover records with a 60-second %7%.

Stated objectives: **%8% 15 minutes, %9% 5 seconds**. The failover has been tested once, nine months ago.

At 08:12 on a weekday, eu-west-1 begins showing elevated API error rates across several %10% services. The %11% Health Dashboard shows an investigation opened for one service in that region. Your error rate is 22% and climbing. Health starts at 100%; this is the final boss.
w7.boss.win:
Ledger survived a regional impairment with 38 minutes of degradation and 2 seconds of data loss, and came out with a DR practice that is tested rather than assumed.

Every world showed up: incident command and blameless analysis (World 4), %1% and non-idempotent job discipline (World 5), budget arithmetic driving the failover decision (World 1), honest status communication (World 6), and the static-stability and %2%/%3% reasoning of this world. The failure that nearly sank you was not the provider event; it was a latent assumption nobody had exercised in nine months.

**Takeaway:** disaster recovery is not an architecture. It is a rehearsal schedule.
w7.boss.lose:
The regional event became a data-integrity incident, a cascade in the standby, or a team that learned nothing. Typical failure paths: failing over before establishing the picture, waiting on a provider ETA, restoring a 9-hour-old backup against a 5-second %1%, scaling instead of shedding, restarting a non-idempotent settlement job, failing back the same day, or ending with a %2% aimed at an absent engineer.

Revisit lessons 7.1, 7.3 and 7.4, plus World 5 lesson 3, and retry.
w7.boss.s0.text:
Pages are firing. The team channel has four hypotheses. Your monitoring dashboards are themselves hosted with resources scoped to eu-west-1, and two panels are not loading.

First move?
w7.boss.s0.c0.text: Declare the incident, take IC, assign Ops and Comms, open the incident doc, and immediately establish what you can still observe: use the standby region's dashboards and the %1% Health Dashboard to separate "our problem" from "provider event".
w7.boss.s0.c0.fb: Command first, then establish observability. Knowing whether this is a provider event changes every subsequent decision, and you need a picture you can trust before choosing a mitigation.
w7.boss.s0.c1.text: Start the regional failover immediately; error rate is 22%.
w7.boss.s0.c1.fb: Failover is a large, partly untested action with an %1% cost. Twenty-two percent is bad but you have not yet established whether it is a provider event, whether it is worsening, or whether a cheaper mitigation exists.
w7.boss.s0.c2.text: Debug the failing service in eu-west-1 to find the root cause.
w7.boss.s0.c2.fb: Root-causing a provider impairment is not available to you, and you are the IC. Mitigate and coordinate.
w7.boss.s1.text: Confirmed: %1% has acknowledged a service impairment in eu-west-1 affecting the service your compute layer depends on. Your error rate is now 41%. %2% replication lag to eu-central-1 reads 0.8 s. Comms asks what to tell customers; the CTO asks whether to fail over.
w7.boss.s1.c0.text: Decide on the arithmetic: at 41% errors the budget burn is extreme, the impairment is provider-side with no ETA, replication lag is within %1%, so fail over. Have Comms post a factual update with a next-update time while Ops executes the %2%.
w7.boss.s1.c0.fb: The decision criteria were pre-agreed: provider event, no ETA, lag within %1%, burn far above what the budget can absorb. Deciding explicitly and communicating on a cadence is the IC's job.
w7.boss.s1.c1.text: Wait for %1% to provide an ETA before deciding.
w7.boss.s1.c1.fb: Provider ETAs during an active investigation are rarely available and rarely accurate. You are burning a month of %1% every few minutes while waiting for someone else to decide for you.
w7.boss.s1.c2.text: Fail over, and post "we are experiencing issues with a third-party provider" to the status page.
w7.boss.s1.c2.fb: The failover call is right, but the message deflects blame instead of telling customers what they need: what is broken, what you are doing, and when the next update comes.
w7.boss.s2.text: Ops begins the %1%. Step 3 fails: promoting the %2% global cluster requires a %3% key that was created as a single-region key in eu-west-1, and the encrypted snapshots in eu-central-1 cannot be read. Someone suggests restoring from the nightly backup in the standby region instead, which is 9 hours old.
w7.boss.s2.c0.text: Check whether the %1% global secondary is itself readable (global databases replicate to a cluster encrypted with a regional key in the target region) before reaching for a 9-hour-old backup; escalate to %2% Support in parallel. A 9-hour %3% against a 5-second objective is a last resort, not a next step.
w7.boss.s2.c0.fb: Correct sequencing: verify the replicated path before abandoning it, escalate in parallel, and treat a 6,000× %1% miss as the last option. The %2% gap itself is a top %3% finding.
w7.boss.s2.c1.text: Restore from the 9-hour-old backup immediately to get service back fast.
w7.boss.s2.c1.fb: You would meet %1% by destroying %2%: nine hours of payments data gone, which for a ledger is worse than being down. Down is recoverable; silently wrong balances are not.
w7.boss.s2.c2.text: Halt the failover and wait for eu-west-1 to recover.
w7.boss.s2.c2.fb: Abandoning the failover on the first obstacle leaves you fully down with no plan and no ETA.
w7.boss.s3.text: The global secondary is readable and promotes successfully; data loss is about 2 seconds. %1% failover records shift traffic. But eu-central-1 was sized as a %2% at 30% of production capacity, and %3% is now trying to add capacity. Error rate in the standby is 18% and latency is climbing.
w7.boss.s3.c0.text: Shed load immediately while capacity grows: enable rate limiting at the edge, disable batch and non-critical workloads, and serve degraded (read-only or queued) responses for the least critical operations. Scaling is minutes away; shedding is seconds away.
w7.boss.s3.c0.fb: World 5's lesson under real conditions. You cannot scale your way out of the next four minutes, and letting the standby cascade would turn a partial recovery into a total outage.
w7.boss.s3.c1.text: Wait for %1% to catch up; capacity is on the way.
w7.boss.s3.c1.fb: Four minutes of 18% errors and rising, with retries amplifying. The standby follows eu-west-1 into a cascade and you have nowhere left to go.
w7.boss.s3.c2.text: Fail back to eu-west-1 since the standby cannot cope.
w7.boss.s3.c2.fb: Failing back into an actively impaired region, after a promotion, with a now-diverged database. This is how a bad day becomes a data-integrity incident.
w7.boss.s4.text: Shedding worked; capacity caught up; error rate is 0.4% and falling. Total impact so far: 38 minutes of degradation, %1% missed by 23 minutes, %2% met at 2 seconds. Ops asks about the batch settlement job that was mid-run in eu-west-1 when the impairment began. Its status is unknown.
w7.boss.s4.c0.text: Do not restart it blind. Establish idempotency first: check the job's checkpoint or ledger entries to determine what completed, and only then reprocess the remaining range. Assign it to Planning to track as a divergence from normal operation.
w7.boss.s4.c0.fb: A settlement job is the least idempotent thing you own. World 5's cron lesson: when in doubt about a non-idempotent job, reconcile before acting, and track the divergence so it is not forgotten at handoff.
w7.boss.s4.c1.text: Restart the job in eu-central-1 to catch up.
w7.boss.s4.c1.fb: Double-settling payments. The financial and trust cost of that exceeds the entire outage.
w7.boss.s4.c2.text: Leave it until after the incident and deal with it tomorrow.
w7.boss.s4.c2.fb: Untracked divergences are how incidents produce second incidents. Track it now, even if you act on it later.
w7.boss.s5.text: %1% reports eu-west-1 recovered. The CTO wants to fail back this afternoon "to get back to normal". Traffic is stable in eu-central-1, which is now scaled to full capacity.
w7.boss.s5.c0.text: Do not fail back under time pressure on the same day. Schedule it as a planned, rehearsed change once the data reconciliation is complete and eu-west-1 has been stable for an agreed period, using the same progressive approach.
w7.boss.s5.c0.fb: Failback is a second failover with a diverged dataset, performed by an exhausted team. There is no operational reason it must happen today; "back to normal" is a feeling, not a requirement.
w7.boss.s5.c1.text: Fail back this afternoon while the team still has context.
w7.boss.s5.c1.fb: A tired team, an untested reverse path, and unreconciled data. The failback becomes the second incident.
w7.boss.s5.c2.text: Stay in eu-central-1 permanently and make eu-west-1 the new standby.
w7.boss.s5.c2.fb: Defensible in principle and worth discussing, but it is an architecture decision made mid-incident by an exhausted team. Decide it in the %1%.
w7.boss.s6.text: You are writing it up. Impact: 38 minutes degraded, 2 seconds of data loss, %1% missed. The room wants to focus on the %2% key that was created single-region eighteen months ago by someone who has since left.
w7.boss.s6.c0.text: Name the systemic causes: DR %1% untested for 9 months, standby sized at 30% with no load test, dashboards scoped to the primary region, no automated check that DR prerequisites (keys, quotas, pipeline) are valid, and no scheduled failover exercise. Action items with owners and dates, plus a standing game-day schedule.
w7.boss.s6.c0.fb: Every one of those would have surfaced the %1% gap before the incident. The %2%'s job is to find the process that let a latent failure survive eighteen months, not the commit that created it.
w7.boss.s6.c1.text: Focus the %1% on the %2% key configuration and how it was approved.
w7.boss.s6.c1.fb: Blame directed at an absent engineer, and a single fix that leaves every other untested DR assumption in place. The next failover finds the next gap.
w7.boss.s6.c2.text: Conclude that the provider impairment was the root cause and the response worked as designed.
w7.boss.s6.c2.fb: The response missed %1% by 150% because of your own untested assumptions. Attributing everything to the provider discards the entire learning opportunity.
